Section: Query Type 2 · B. Data Refresh Frequency
Original copy:
We recommend Monthly or Weekly Data Refresh for Topical Queries. Both save money yet are adequate for studying big categorical changes. Brands studying category trends are typically studying the bigger picture as opposed to what happened yesterday or even last week.

If you choose Monthly Refresh, we'll pull data on the 2nd of every month, re-augment the searches based on new content that's appeared since the last query, and send you back the month's videos by the 5th. Anytime your clients visit your platform from the 6th through the last day of the month, they'll be looking at data that's fresh through the end of the prior month. For brands studying big picture category shifts and looking for new trends, Monthly Refresh is perfectly acceptable. We've discounted it to deal with the high cost of Contextual Topic Queries.

If you choose Weekly Data Refresh you will save money, but your users will face a data hole that's miniscule on Mondays and awkwardly large on Sundays. We pull weekly data on Sunday nights, collecting the prior week's Monday to Sunday activity. If a user visits on a Monday, the data is completely current - the entire past week is available to them. The user who logs in on a Thursday will notice this week's Monday to Wednesday data is missing. The user who logs in on Sunday will face an entire week of missing data. Generally speaking, the weeklong data gap has no impact on brands studying Topics.

If you choose Daily Data Refresh, your users will always have new data through yesterday, no matter when they visit your platform. New data includes any new Videos or Comments that appeared yesterday, as well as fresh metric counts (like new views) on older evergreen videos. Daily Refresh is best for Brand Queries, where monitoring new product rollouts, tracking organic pickup of time-sensitive campaigns like Super Bowl, monitoring media pickup of PR initiatives, tracking Crisis PR situations and closely monitoring consumer complaints is the need. Daily Refresh would be overkill for most Topical Searches.

Original copy:
Adjusted Queries: We perform basic changes to dramatically improve search results. Programmatically, as the query comes in, we change apostrophes and quotations to our universal format, and we remove punctuation (except apostrophes) and hashtags. Manually, we combine terms that aren't combined and we split terms that are combined. For example, if the query says "Glassskin" we add "Glass Skin," catching significantly more videos. Where OR strings are connected by the wrong operator, we fix it. We add all the possessives and plurals. If the user has submitted more than one brand in the query we remove the second brand and submit a second query for your approval. If there are obvious, easy things we can to do improve the catch or discard the noise in the few minutes allowed, we do it.

Contextual Queries are 100% Accurate and Complete, and we guarantee it. It's the Mercedes of Social Listening. If you can afford this option, Contextual is the way to go. Your clients will immediately notice your mastery of Video Social Listening. To achieve perfection, we combine our big data engineering with People Power - the same people who've classified every YouTube brand video into hundreds of thousands of topical homes. Our people aren't guessing at terms. They're looking at the entire database of videos that responds to the query. They can see - and are aided by AI to see - the thousands of Boolean operators needed to NOT OUT the NOISE and CATCH all the SIGNAL.

Some platforms have expressed nervousness around this, concerned we might make judgment calls the brand wouldn't agree with. Things are surprisingly black and white. Incoming queries very clearly state the brands' intentions. The problem is that users never achieve their stated intention. There are never enough NOTs, ANDs and ORs to get the job done. We expand terms and channels to find every video matching the brand's criteria. We take out all the Noise. Example: Orange Telecom submits "Orange AND Phone." A video entitled "Get your newest phone at the local Orange store" is Signal. A kids' cartoon with the knock knock joke, "Orange you glad I didn't call you on the phone?" is Noise. The lines are easy to draw, but to get good results, someone needs to draw them. Without the actual database of content to work with, that's impossible to do.

Our Contextual Queries contain 1,000 to 10,000 operators per query and produce 5–50× more results than Adjusted Queries. Contextual queries are the only way to go for generic-name brands like Orange Telecom, Dodge Cars, Specialized Bicycles, Columbia Sportswear, Liberty Financial. Contextual Queries are perfected by Day 30, but they're also never done. New content reveals new combinations of words that beg for more NOTs, ANDs and ORs.

At a $2mm spending level, our Contextual Queries become your property so you can use them to improve results on TikTok, Reels and elsewhere.

Original copy:
Everyone asks the same question. Why won't YouTube give us enough quota to report accurately on their medium? We agree that the lack of YouTube results in Social Listening has had a direct effect on YouTube revenues, and we hope to contribute to fixing that. But more quota wouldn't help the platforms. The problem is database structure. YouTube is not a classic search engine like Google. Google wants to give you what you want right away - no need for a Page 2. YouTube, on the other hand, wants to increase users' Watch Time. That's why search results are filled with irrelevant content. That's why queries bring back more noise than signal.

We've been testing brand queries for a few months now. The average query submitted to the YouTube Search API brings back about 300 videos. Of those 300 videos, fewer than 10 videos on average satisfy the query. That's a 97% noise ratio. When we Adjust the brand's query with our fastest fix, those 10 on-target videos grow into the thousands. When we Contextualize the Query and eliminate all noise, we produce tens of thousands on Pure Signal videos over the 10 found via the YouTube API. The difference is astounding.

"Why won't YouTube give us enough API quota to report accurately on their medium?" Everyone asks.  

Let's be clear:  more YouTube quota won't help the platforms extract better Social Listening Results. The problem is two-fold: database structure on YouTube's end, and blind query-writing on the platforms' end.  

YouTube Search is a recommendation engine, not a search engine in the classic sense.  YouTube Search aims to expose users to new content that will enhance how much time people spend on the platform.  That's why query-ing the YouTube Search API brings back more noise than signal.   Part One of one of Touchstorm DataLabs' solution is technical.  We boil the entire YouTube ocean for all content, parse out the brands, and classify them in a structure that can accurately respond to Social Listening queries.  

The second part of our solution is query improvement.  This component is human, although AI is speeding up human production.  Query-writing without a content database is a blind exercise.  Previewing query results against real-life data takes the blinders off.  That advantage belongs solely to Touchstorm DataLabs.

Original copy: Social Listening Platforms either have clients write their own queries, and/or, the platform expands them using AI. Our extensive testing reveals that when these queries hit the YouTube search API the results produced are 95% noise and 5% signal on average. That's because YouTube wants other things out of its Search Engine, and therefore, fills results with recommended Videos that don't answer brands' Social Listening Queries. You're unable to publish great results, and in turn, that hurts YouTube, because virtually every brand - also an advertiser - sees their best results coming from Meta and other properties. Touchstorm DataLabs is the only company to have pre-configured YouTube's database so that it can be queried by Social Listening Platforms and brands interested in gathering their own Social Listening Data. Every video ever made about a brand - whether the brand name is in the Video Title or buried deep within a Description, Tag or Transcript - has been classified into our marketing taxonomy, the Touchstorm Video Index. Brands, and each of their divisions, live in precisely the right categories & sub-categories. Videos made about brands by others live precisely inside hundreds of thousands of Topics and Sub-Topics. Product Information has its home as well.
